Dear Sam: 

What a pity you had to miss the Camping Conference this year. I 
think you who have seen this thing grow would have been even more 
impressed than I was. Each year it gets bigger and better. We, of course, 
maintained our usual popularity by serving coffee as fast as it could be 
poured — 600 cups (!) — but I still have to refuse to go along with your 
thoroughly vulgar suggestion that we should christen it “Kert’s Koffee 
Korner”. 

The big thing this year is DANDY, a really extraordinary liquid 
detergent. It is much the most concentrated product of its kind and it is 
almost impervious to contamination. This means that you can wash many, 
many greasy dishes before it becomes necessary to change the water. All this 
adds up to a very economical cleaner. I think the Camps are going to like it, 
especially as we are supplying free of charge a simple, but completely 
effective, dispenser, which just screws into the top of the gallon bottles 
and measures out exactly one ounce — enough for a normal sink — and 
ensures that there will be no wasteage. Our friends at the Royal York 
went away bearing samples of DANDY, which they will now have tried 
and, I am sure, thoroughly approved. I am going to send you a sample to 
prove it to yourself. If you know of anyone else who would like one, get 
them to drop me a line and I will certainly see that they get enough to 
carry out a thorough test. 

You will be pleased to know that we have decided to handle the paint 
line, which you found so good last year. Frankly I was a little doubtful 
until I saw your dark green cabins so effectively painted over with only 
one coat of white. We have since used it in our own plant, and I can 
confirm your good opinions, first hand. These Selectone paints should go 
very well this year. We are buying in very large quantities and will have 
the pleasure of offering the whole line to our Camping friends at Dealers 
Prices — they will thus have the opportunity of buying at Hardware Store 
COSTS. 

The new trucking set-up I was telling you about is now in operation 
and we shall be delivering this year to most Camps on our own Transports, 
which will produce a significant price saving, of which our Camps will get 
full benefit. 

Looking forward to seeing you again very soon, I am, 

With warmest personal regards, 

J. S. Hearn, 

JSH/owi 


Toronto, Canada, April, 1957

EDITORIAL 


By W. E. Yard 


Our world in 1957 is a world of 
headlines,—big , bold, shocking, some¬ 
times terrifying, headlines. 

Young people are frequently confused 
by these headlines as they try desper¬ 
ately to fit themselves for useful roles 
in our society. 

Camp counsellors and staff took time 
at a recent O.C.A. counsellor training 
meeting to ask themselves where, in 
camp work, were the opportunities re¬ 
lated to alleviating the problems and 
conditions which so often dominate the 
headlines ... It was a positive 
discussion, for there are opportunities— 
and our young people saw them some¬ 
thing like this: 

Related to the World Situation . . . 
We, at camp, have opportunities for 
music, games, special “international” 
programmes, worship services and fund¬ 
raising projects for various missionary 
works . . . and through all of these, 
to build, above all, a spirit of under¬ 
standing and brotherhood in large 
groups of children among whom are 
certainly those with potentials for lead¬ 
ing our world towards universal peace 
and goodwill. 

Related to tragedies that result from 
emotional instability . . . We, at 

camp, have opportunities for providing 
security, love and outlets for creative 
expression, and through these, to help 
young people in their normal emotional 
development. . . . We also have an 
opportunity to detect problems at an 
early stage and to assist parents in 
securing the most helpful advice when 
such problems become apparent. 


Related to “Teenage” Headlines —We, 
at camp, have perhaps the greatest 
opportunity of all. Recognizing the 
special group and individual needs of 
these fast-growing boys and girls, we 
can provide a setting which has at once 
the picturesque attractiveness and out¬ 
standing leadership to which they best 
respond, the opportunities for physical 
“proving” that they need and want, 
and the sense of “independence” that 
helps them grow through away-from- 
homc experience. 

Related to the changing conditions 
of work — (i.e. shorter week, more 
leisure time) — We camp people have 
one of our most important challenges 
in helping young people acquire the 
interests, applications, skills, and atti¬ 
tudes which will have positive “carry 
over value” in later years. Not the 
least of these is a positive attitude 
toward work itself, so aptly expressed 
by the late David Lloyd George: 

“Work you have accomplished is the 
only real legacy you can leave to the 
world. It can be a worth-while legacy 
if you choose to make it so. Find 
some task into which you can throw 
your whole heart and soul; and hav¬ 
ing found it, learn to do that task as 
thoroughly and efficiently as possible. 
Opportunities for great things come 
surely to one who is reliable, efficient 
and eager. But let your purpose be 
the doing of the job, not the reward 
of fame to he reaped therefrom; for 
the final measure of a man is not 
what he has gained, but what he has 
done.” —• 


Toronto , Canada , April , 1957 


15 



THE COUNSELLOR'S JOB 


One thing all directors have to face 
is the fact that there is no source of 
trained counsellors. There is no central 
supply house where he can order a 
dozen counsellors trained to look after 
cabin groups. There are no annual 
“graduating” classes of people who 
have had a three- or four-year course 
in camp counselling. He must gather 
together people who have the basic 
personalities, and train them himself. 
He must run concurrently, a camp for 
children and a training school for their 
leaders. 

He has set up this training scheme. 
It is a long-term project in his eyes 
... a matter of years, perhaps. 

How does it work? How do you 
become trained? When do you become 
trained? Pre pre-camp, pre-camp, all 
summer? Part of your job is making 
the best use of this training. 

Your contract — When you sign 
your contract you are joining an organ¬ 
ization pledging yourself to it. 

Your duties fall into several areas of 
responsibility: — 

1st AREA:—Your duties in association 
with the Director. 

A. Become Oriented: 

l.Find out the philosophy of the 
Gamp—its aims, ideals, objectives, 
standards, etc. —• 

How do you do this? 


a. Printed statement 

b. Ask questions 

c. Keep your eyes and ears open 
— everything that is done in 
this camp reflects its philo¬ 
sophy. 

2. Become physically oriented: — 
Explore the place: — 

Buildings and their names 

Equipment 

The natural environment—trees, 

rocks, etc. Become familiar with 

it. Learn to live in the woods. 

Keep healthy, warm and dry. 

3. Rules and Regulations: — 

Learn them. Most come under two 
headings:—• 

1. Safety 

2. The solution for a problem 
which the camp has faced. 

What do you do if you find your¬ 
self in disagreement with the rules 
and regulations? 

1. Just keep quiet for a few days, 
and acquiesce. Go through 
the motions. 

2. Examine the reasons. 

3. Think over the aims and 
ideals. Do you agree with 
them? 

If, after due consideration you 
can find no adequate reason for 
them, or, if you feel that they are 
all wrong, then complain where 
you will get results. Muttering 


16 


Canadian Camping 



AT CAMP 


• • • • • 




br¬ 


and grumbling gets you nowhere 
—• go to the director and state 
your case. Then, when you accept 
these things as reasonable, show 
it by your conduct. This means 
you — not your sisters and your 
cousins and your aunts. Be a true 
citizen—with a positive approach. 

B. Work — Evaluation and Criticism: 

Expect and accept this —it is 
necessary. Most camps have some 
sort of set-up for this:—interviews, 
blanks filled out, observation. 

Directors develop a sort of extra¬ 
sensory perception. During one week: 

1. If the director meets your cabin 
members gathered in a glum little 
group, obviously engaged in troub¬ 
led conversation; 

2. If all the things in the lost and 
found box belong to you and your 
cabin group; 

3. If the light in your cabin is still 
blazing, and sounds of revelry are 
issuing forth after Taps; 

4. If your children are standing near 
the dock shivering and waiting to 
go swimming — when you finally 
arrive; 

5. If your table in the dining-room is 
noisy and littered; 

6. If the director receives long-dis¬ 
tance calls from worried parents 
who haven’t had a letter or post¬ 
card from their children; 

7. If none of your children are wear¬ 
ing rain-coats on a rainy day. 


Mrs. Ralph H. Raymer 
Director, Camp Tanamakoon 


If all of these things occur, he 
knows you need guidance. 

You should expect constructive 
criticism. You should receive helpful 
suggestions which will point the way 
to improving your work. 

Be teachable. Sometimes these 
things hurt. Sometimes it hurts to 
grow. But be willing to try out the 
advice you get. 

C. Problem Solving: 

Put your brains to work. Problems 
don’t have to be accepted passively. 
Most of them have a solution some¬ 
where. (I’ll throw out one you can 
think over: what should be done to 
prevent food parcels from being sent 
to or smuggled into the camp?). 
You may win the director’s everlast¬ 
ing gratitude. 


There have been many requests for a 
reprint of Mrs. Raymer 3 s lecture at the 
Orientation Course for Camp Counsellors at 
the University of Toronto, Department of 
University Extension. We present it to our 
readers as a check-list for Directors or 
Counsellors. 


Toronto, Canada, April, 1957 


17 



The director is your backer. He is 
the one who can help you with your 
problems—but don’t expect him to 
be a mind reader. And don’t let 
your problem get big before you ask 
for help. 

If you are asked to go in for an 
interview — GO. 

D. Reports and Paper Work: 

In the parent’s eyes, the director 
is personally responsible for every 
child in camp. Obviously one adult 
cannot look after all those children. 
Keep the director informed, through 
; various channels he has created for 
.this purpose. 

He can do things for you — 

You can do things for him 


E. Care of Equipment.: 

Referring to all equipment—tents, 
cabins, books, canoes, tennis racquets, 
, the plumbing, even knives and forks 
and spoons. They represent the in- 
i vestment of thousands of dollars. 
You can’t have your cake and eat 
it too. If the budget for each year 
must be spent on repairing and re¬ 
placing lost and damaged articles, 
the camp cannot extend its equip¬ 
ment each year. 

There is a peculiar kind of van¬ 
dalism which seems to be inherent 
in human beings which becomes 
apparent in the great out-of-doors. 
Cutting bark from trees, strewing 
refuse about, dumping garbage in 
the lake, carving names on cabin 
walls, slitting canvas with a knife, 
using canoes for benches, throwing 
the dishes away instead of washing 
them. We are doing our future citi¬ 


zens a favor when we teach them not 

to be vandals. 

F. Public Relations: 

1. Visitors expect a cheerful word 

of greeting, or a nod. _ _ 

2. Parents expect to meet you when 
they come to camp. Don’t run 
and hide. Remember, they love 
Johnny. Remember, they are stuck 
with Johnny for a long time to 
come — give them a ray of hope. 

3. Time off: You are representing 
the camp, (remember when you 
signed your contract). Behave so 
that the general public feels — 
“that must be a good camp”. 

4. The trunk that goes home at the 
end of the summer . . . tidy it, 
send clothes home in a presentable 
condition. 


2nd Area — Maintenance Staff 

Get a concept of who does what in 
the camp. 

Who gives the cooks their orders? 

Who gives the caretakers theirs? 
Find out how one gets something 
done around the place. Some of it 
you can do yourself. 

1. Learn their names. 

2. Treat them with courtesy. 

4. Let them get on with their work. 

3. Show appreciation of their work. 

Don’t waste their time. 

An influx of unexpected guests 
can demoralize any kitchen — at 
home or at camp. Most directors 
would exchange any number of coun¬ 
sellors for one good cook. 


18 


Canadian Camping 


3rd Area — Other Counsellors: 3. Lend a helping hand. 


Now find out where you fit in. To 
whom are you responsible? Obviously 
the director can’t manage all details, 
so there are Section Heads, Activity 
Heads, etc. 

A. Living and Working with others — 
your own peers. 

1. Pitfalls: 

1. Gossip (the grapevine) 

2. Borrowing: 

(a) Personal 

(b) Camp equipment 

3. Untidiness — living quarters, 
elsewhere. 

4. Telling other people how to do 
their jobs. 

5. Noise 

6. Exclusive friendships 

7. Letting George Do It. 

8. Practical jokes 

9. Tardiness 

10. “Center staging it” 

(a) as an individual on the 
program. 

(b) your activity 

2. How to be popular in one easv 
lesson. You’ve heard it before. Put 
yourself in the other person’s place 
— “Do unto others”. 

1. Be considerate. 

2. Be a professional staff member. 
Back up your fellow workers 
with your enthusiasm and loyalty. 


4. Keep your possessions collected. 

5. Uphold policies you have helped 
formulate or agreed to. 

6. Help the new counsellors. 

7. Keep yourself in good condition. 

Part of this job is learning to be 
a member of a group. Let’s face 
it. For most of us life is a group 
experience. There is still room for 
you to be an individual — no one 
wants to warp your personality, 
but getting along with others is 
the first qualification for all jobs. 

3. Time off: 

1. Remember that your job is im¬ 
portant. See that all details will 
be looked after while you are 
absent. 

2. Remember that the camp cannot 
operate efficiently or adequately 
without a staff. This may re¬ 
quire some adaptability on your 
part. 


4th Area — and the most important of 
all: — THE CHILDREN 

Pause for a moment and go back to 
the beginning — philosophy. Ask your¬ 
self — “Why does this camp exist?” 

“The Camp is for the Campers” — 
Never forget this for one minute. 

What do we do for these campers? 

A. As a counsellor your job will include 
all the little details of every day life; 
much of it will be an educating pro¬ 
cess: 


Toronto , Canada , April , 1957 


19 


1. How to make a bed—maybe how 
to get into one. 

2. How to use a broom or polish a 
lantern. 

3. How to write a letter. 

4. How to wash themselves: be 
thankful pigtails are not so stylish 
now. 

5. How to change clothes—or wear 
the proper ones for the weather. 

6. How to tidy trunks and check 

- trunk clothing lists. 

7. How to. deal, with a wet bed. 

8. When to send a child to the 
nurse, or to the doctor. 

9. Quiet—rest hour and after Taps; 
remember the camp is for the 
campers. 

10. Dining room — manners; noise; 
eating habits; singing; running in 
arid out. : > 

All of this is on a graded scale 
depending on whether the child is 
six or sixteen. 


B. It will include teaching activities: 

1. Know the material yourself. 

2. Know how to teach it. 

3. Make it attractive: — motiva¬ 
tion (five senses). Challenge them, 
make them want to learn. 

4. Let them learn. You are cheating 
the children if you do it all your¬ 
self. i.e. Going on a cookout, and 
doing all the cooking. 


20 


5. Concentrate on the pupils; don’t 
frustrate them. Be on time . . . 
and teach, 

6. You will probably teach in a field 
other than your own. e.g. — the 
music counsellor on a cook-out; 
the canoeing counsellor leading a 
sing-song. 

And if you are teaching swim¬ 
ming, sailing, archery, chopping, 
whittling, etc., never take your eyes 
off them for a moment. Camping 
is full of life and death situations. 

7. You will be expected to be able to 
help your group plan for rainy 
days; have ideas for special events; 
know things to do for an evening 
programme; how to run a party. 

-.1 ' 

C. You will be expected to know and 

understand your campers: 

1. Learn their names. 

(a) Incidentally, don’t fall into 
the habit of speaking of the 
children in derogatory terms. 
If you call them “little mon¬ 
sters” often enough, you may 
begin to think of them as little 
monsters, and treat them as 
little monsters. This is applic¬ 
able too to derogatory nick¬ 
names. People going through 
life with a nickname such as 
“Ape”, “Monkey-face”, “Hip¬ 
po”, “Carrot-top”, are being 
saddled with a burden which 
may colour their attitudes to¬ 
ward life. 

2. It is not exactly correct to think 
of yourself as a temporary parent. 
You are not the parent of these 
children. There is an emotional 
involvement in parenthood which 


Canadian Camping 


colours the thinking and makes it 
almost impossible to look at a 
child objectively. 

(a) “Just like his Father” “just 
like his mother”. 

(b) “You are our child—you can¬ 
not get poor marks in school”. 

You, as a counsellor, are in a 
much more fortunate position for 
observing that child. You see him 
living with a group of his peers. 
Few parents ever have this oppor¬ 
tunity. You see him without the 
cloak of self-consciousness that he 
wears when in his parents’ pres¬ 
ence. (e.g. you yourselves “Act 
differently”, at camp than you do 
at home). You are providing the 
protection and the loving interest 
that is found in the home, but vou 
are also giving this child an oppor¬ 
tunity to test out his independence, 
a chance to see what he can do as 
an individual. 

You will agree — no two chil¬ 
dren are alike. But — do you put 
this knowledge into practice? 

Learn to know children — use 
their trick of observation. Go with 
them to evening programmes, 
watch how they act and react. Go 
for walks with them and listen to 
their conversation. Watch the 
the group getting ready for a stunt 
night, or a tidying the cabin. En¬ 
courage conversation at the table 
— and listen. Learn what activi¬ 
ties appeal to them and how they 
are getting along. 


3. Children are human beings. They 
may be small, but they have the 
same basic needs that you have. 
They need recognition, affection, 
belonging to the group, achieve¬ 


ment. They need to feel that they 
are living in a democracy. 

Maybe you can decide for your¬ 
self what he needs to get from 
camp. But turn the coin over. 
Have you found out what he, the 
camper, the individual, the person 
wants to get out of camp. What 
are his hopes and dreams? These 
too, are his needs. Ask a fifteen 
year old and you get a list — a ten 
year old and you get “Fun”. 

Sometimes it helps to sketch a 
little picture, remember what you 
were like at that age. Say to your¬ 
self, I am ten years old. I am in 
Grade five. My teacher is Miss 
Jones. Life is full of fun and prob¬ 
lems. Your clothes had to be like 
those of everyone else. You were 
quick to sense justice and injustice 
in your leaders. You expected them 
to be patient and explain things 
over and over again, until you 
understood them. You expected 
your “share” of everything going 
on. (Like dealing out a pack of 
cards). You expected your exalted 
leader to see whether it was a ball 
or a strike, and you let him know 
in no uncertain terms when he 
called a fair hit a foul ball. Now 
quickly, before you lose that feel¬ 
ing say to yourself — “How would 
I like my counsellor to treat me if 
I were ten years old, and in this 
cabin group?”. Now you are learn¬ 
ing to put yourself in the child’s 
place. 

Now go a step further — and 
really forget about yourself and 
put yourself in his place. Be the 
kind of counsellor he needs. “Do 
unto others” — again.

AMONG 

OURSELVES 


By John Halcrow 

General Manager, 
London YM - YWCA 


The Reader’s Digest Magazine has 
presented many interesting “most un¬ 
forgettable characters.” Each person can 
think of his own “most unforgettable 
character.” In this article on C. T. 
Sharpe I present my “most unforget¬ 
table character” or my “most likeable 
character” or my most remarkable char¬ 
acter” or my-anyway an excellent 

fellow, as many people will agree. I 
appreciate the invitation to write this 
article. 

Twenty-four hours after I had met 
C. T. Sharpe, school teacher, camping 
enthusiast, and ex-YMCA secretary, I 
stood on the Orillia Railway Station 
platform with him. In his pocket was a 
telegram from a student of some years 
back. The student was to have a ten 
minute train stop at Orillia during a 
longer trip. 

The train seemed barely in when a 
handsome,enthusiastic young fellow was 
rushing up the platform toward us. 
The young fellow, grasping “C.T.” by 


CHARTERS T. SHARPE 


the hand, fairly shouted, “Where’s vour 
second handkerchief?” Quickly “C. T.” 
produced two handkerchiefs and chal¬ 
lenged the young fellow he called John¬ 
ny. Later I learned this was a rule from 
school days which required each stu¬ 
dent to cam- a spare handkerchief. 

The life of Charters T. Sharpe has 
been made up of many kind acts, inter¬ 
esting experiences, humorous incidents 
and innumerable friends. I have known 
him for over twenty-five years. He was 
born in Toronto—and is proud of it. 
Some friends know “C. T.” has a twin 
sister. Many know he had three sisters 
and one brother, each of them proud 
of our hero. 

As a boy he attended Givens Street 
School, and in his spare time could 
frequently be found at West End 
YMCA. He obtained a part-time job 
as a parcel boy at the T. Eaton Com¬ 
pany. Probably the Manager of the 



22 


Canadian Camping 


Parcelling Department still has night¬ 
mares when he recalls those days. It is 
recorded that our hero had a willing 
spirit, but too many thumbs — or at 
least fingers which worked like thumbs. 

Having overcome a difficult start, 
“C. T.” decided that he should abandon 
education to enter the world of busi¬ 
ness. Unknown to her son, Mrs. Sharpe 
visited the West End YMCA Boys’ 
Work Secretary, and obtained his co¬ 
operation to keep the wavering student 
at his studies. “C. T.” still refers to 
the kindly, but adroit way, this “Y” 
Secretary persuaded him to stay at 
school. Many times in public speeches 
“C. T.” has stated, “Anything I can do 
for the YMCA will not be adequate to 
repay what the “Y” has done for me”. 
The foregoing expresses the apprecia¬ 
tion and loyalty of C. T. Sharpe for 
good organizations and worthy causes. 

In 1909, Orillia secured the young 
fellow of our article to make him the 
first Boys’ Secretary of the town’s 
YMCA and one of the early pioneers in 
organized Boys’ Work. He served Tor¬ 
onto West End YMCA in the same 
capacity during the 1912 to 1915 period. 
Many men now successfully established, 
including the Premier of Ontario, The 
Honourable Leslie Frost, recall happv 
and progressive “Y” days under Boys’ 
Secretary Sharpe. 

At the outbreak of war in 1914 
“C. T.” offered his services and in 1915 
was directed into the YMCA War 
Services. He served with distinction in 
England, France and Belgium through¬ 
out the war, with rank of Captain, 
heading up the difficult task of serving 
the very widely-dispersed Canadian 
Railway Troops. When the war ended 
most men were in a rush to return to 
Canada, but “C. T.” accepted a call 
to remain overseas on a clean-up job. 
He travelled extensively in England and 
on the Continent on this work. 


Month’s after the war’s end, back in 
Canada, a decision had to be made 
between taking further education or 
immediately re-entering YMCA work. 
A selection of the educational oppor¬ 
tunities later led him into the teaching 
profession. 

Boys of widely varying appearance, 
size, temperament and intelligence 
passed through the usually gentle, but 
when necessary, very firm hands of this 
teacher. He taught for twenty years at 
the Toronto Normal Model School, 
seven years at the University of Tor¬ 
onto Schools, and for three years, just 
prior to retirement in 1951, was the 
Government’s first full-time Director 
of Camping for Ontario. His classes 
were patterned to some extent along the 
lines of the great schools of England, 
but enriched with many unorthodox 
and wonderful individual touches. Some 
are well worth the recounting. Possibly 
better than any other way these anec¬ 
dotes reveal the character of this “most 
unforgettable character.” 

It was just prior to a Pancake Tues¬ 
day that I was invited to the annual 
school recognition of that day. Upon 
arrival I was warmly welcomed and 
directed to a seat along with various 
dignitaries from business, professional 
and educational fields. The room was 
kept clear in the centre except for a 
rope drawn tightly across at a height of 
about six feet. A group of happy, ex¬ 
cited lads lined the walls. One could 
feel the anticipation from this group. 
Finally “C. T.” appeared in the centre 
of the room and appropriately addressed 
the gathering. The boys took places on 
the opposite side of the rope. Suddenly 
there appeared the largest frying pan in 
history, and in the pan the largest 
pancake. “C. T.” accepted the pan 
with great dignity. The boys cheered. 
With a short run, followed by a great 
heave, “C. T.” tossed the pancake high 
in the air and over the rope. Pande- 


T or onto, Canada, April, 1957 


23 


monium broke loose as the boys wildly 
scrambled for handfuls of the giant 
pancake. To eat it might have caused 
indigestion. To get the right handful 
meant riches—it was loaded with many 
coins of various denominations. It was 
a great annual school event. Someday 
before I totter off to the Great Beyond 
I wish I could be a pancake grabber, or 
at least a pancake tosser. Happy mem¬ 
ories for the lucky boys. 

“C. T.” has always maintained high 
personal standards. Often by example, 
conversation, or inducement he has per¬ 
suaded others to set their standards 
higher. He recognizes the harm from 
smoking by juveniles, and frequently 
gives advice. At times he used to take 
a two dollar bill and make an agree¬ 
ment with some lad. Tearing the bill 
in half “C. T.” would give half to the 
selected boy. An agreement was made 
that, if the boy had not smoked by 18 
years of age, he could claim the com¬ 
plete bill, as “C. T.” filed his half away. 
One day a young man telephoned to 
say he would celebrate his 18th birth¬ 
day soon and he had refrained from 
smoking. On his birthday “C. T.” took 
the fellow out to dinner. As a highlight 
of the event, “C. T ” matched the two 
halves of the bill and presented the 
fellow with both, asking what would be 
done with the total of two dollars. To 
“C.T.’s” surprise the young man said, “I 
am going straight to the nearest store 
and buy myself a $2.00 pipe.” When 
asked the brand of tobacco he would 
use the young fellow replied, “I’m not 
going to start to smoke yet, but I earned 
the pipe and I might as well have it.” 

If you meet me sometime and want 
me to reminisce, ask me about the ad¬ 
ventures of C. T. Sharpe. Remind me 
to tell you how “C. T.” mailed a house- 
brick “collect” to a friend in Ottawa; 
how he traded 50*f new ties for $2.50 
ties; where he stuck his big thumb into 


the wet wall finish of a new building; 
when he lost his bags at Sarasota; how 
the hospital officials would not give him 
a dismissal prior to Christmas because 
the hospital needed him to cheer up 
fellow patients at hospital Christmas 
festivities; and how he got on a train 
at Belleville to go to Peterborough and 
was enroute back to Toronto. 

Charters T. Sharpe is a remarkable 
fellow. I have travelled many enjoyable 
miles with him — and hope to travel 
more. I have seen him buy a complete 
row of seats to take young lads to a 
National Hockey League game; give a 
splendid playing field to a Boys’ Camp; 
travel hundreds of miles to do a favour; 
support work in several Churches, and 
spend many hours with a lad who 
needed help to work out a personal 
problem. One time he had strings of 
pennants made up at personal expense 
to loan out without charge to Churches, 
Y’s, Schools, Clubs, etc. He has sent 
out over 2000 Birthday cards per year 
for many years and the recipients really 
appreciate them. 

In 1944 he was elected President of 
Toronto West End YMCA without 
having previously held office. This un¬ 
precedented honour came in the Cen¬ 
tennial Year of the YMCA. For twenty- 
five years he was associated with two of 
Ontario’s well known private camps for 
boys. Earlier he operated YMCA and 
Sunday School Camps. As Director of 
Camping for Ontario he probably vis¬ 
ited more Camps in any one season 
than any man in Canada. 

Being a bachelor, “C. T.” comes and 
goes at his own convenience. He re¬ 
cently went on a six-week trip to 
Europe and was gone nearer to six 
months. His gift to me from each 
country:—a sample of their form of 
licorice. Maybe my later visit in Lon- 

con tinned on page 32

camp for children with an enrolment 
of about fifty campers, the following 
list of supplies may be helpful. Spec¬

of them are local, and doctors attending 
the camp may have individual prefer¬

would at least be satisfactory for the

HOmSICKHiS 

“A Symptom Complex Related to Separation from Home” 

By Dr. Taylor Statten 

Director of Child Psychiatry, 

Montreal Children's Hospital 


This study is made on 75 cases of 
campers in 15 camps considered by their 
directors to be “homesick”. Homesick¬ 
ness can manifest itself in a variety of 
ways. It is often, but not always, re¬ 
lated to being away from home. How¬ 
ever, it may be a means of escaping 
from difficulties in getting along with 
others, or a way of attracting attention 
and manipulating others. It often rep¬ 
resents deeper problems in a child of 
his family relationships. In its most 
natural form it is related to the struggle 
of growing up. It can therefore be 
defined as a symptom complex which 
reflects an underlying emotional state, 
usually depressive, to which the child 
is attempting to adjust. 

Symptoms and Signs 

The most common symptoms were 
“crying”, “loneliness”, and “despond¬ 
ency” which were observed in three- 
quarters of the cases. The most fre¬ 
quent symptoms which appeared in 
approximately one-half the cases was 
the “desire to go home”, “poor appe¬ 
tite” and “inactivity”. It is somewhat 
surprising that the symptom of the 
desire to go home is not more frequent. 
However, we are all very familiar with 
the child who is courageously trying to 
work out his homesick feelings. “Poor 
appetite” and “inactivity” are often the 
first symptoms of physical illness and 
therefore we must not be too hasty in 


considering these as just homesickness 
but must put the responsibility on to 
the medical authorities. I cannot cau¬ 
tion you too much on this point. Child¬ 
ren do develop illness on the way to 
camp, some incubate infectious diseases 
during the first few days or weeks at 
camp. It is a wise administrator who 
insists that all children considered to be 
homesick be checked by the doctor. It 
allows the child to see that his symptoms 
are recognized, taken seriously and that 
he is going to he taken care of no 
matter what the cause of his symptoms 
appears to be. 

There is another important group of 
symptoms which can represent or sug¬ 
gest physical illness, or merely the phys¬ 
ical components of emotional stress and 
anxiety. They were present in approxi¬ 
mately one-fifth of our cases and in 
order of their frequency are: poor sleep, 
abdominal pain, headaches, either con¬ 
stipation or diarrhoea or both, and 
vomiting. It goes without saying that 
these children should be examined by 
a doctor. He can often define the 
problem for the child, in a way that 
will help him come to grips with what 
the underlying cause of his symptoms 
may be, in a way that no non-medical 
person could possibly do. 

Another group of symptoms which 
appear with about the same frequency 
as the above group, i.e., one-fifth to 


26 


Canadian Camping 



one-quarter of the cases, is perhaps the 
most difficult group to handle. These 
are the “feelings of being prosecuted”, 
that “everybody is against him” and 
“that nothing is the way it should be”. 

The other symptoms which have been 
included in the check list are, excessive 
dependency, extreme anxiety, appearing 
in about one-fifth of the cases; and 
aggressiveness, unco-operativeness and 
attention-seeking, which are seen less 
frequently. 

Incidence 

We will now turn our attention to 
the incidence of homesickness. It was 
stated by one observer that all children 
are faced with this problem and that 
we are only aware of those children 
who as yet have been unable to reach 
a satisfactory solution. We see this 
symptom complex but we do not cal/ 
it homesickness. It is a mood or a 
reaction, expressed as disappointment 
or sadness, to some known external 
cause, but where a reaction has been 
set off within the child because the 
present set of circumstances had reactiv¬ 
ated emotions belonging to some traum¬ 
atic situation, such as a separation, in 
the past. So we are not going to put 
a number on the incidence of homesick¬ 
ness. 

It is certain that the amount of 
homesicknes will vary with the basic 
security of our homes and communities, 
children being able to leave home with 
a feeling that they will return to it 
again and find it and their loved ones 
intact and happy. We can say that the 
more we are aware of the existence of 
these symptoms and of their meanings, 
the more likely we are to be able to 
recognize the problem or the potential 
problem. 


A Theoretical Concept 

Can we reach any basis for a better 
understanding of homesickness by con¬ 
sulting the psychiatric literature? The 
description of our homesickness com¬ 
plex resembles the psychiatric sympto¬ 
matology of grief, mourning and depres¬ 
sion. 

It is necessary to turn back a few 
years to the time of the newborn in¬ 
fants, because we belive that many of 
the patterns of behaviour seen in older 
children and adults are derived from 
experiences laid down in those early 
formative years. 

The first interpersonal relationship 
experienced by a human being is the 
mother-baby relationship and through 
it he learns, right from the start, pat¬ 
terns of expecting certain treatment 
and reacting to the treatment. Within 
that relationship he experiences very 
early in life two fundamental emotions. 
For one we use the term “love”, to 
describe a state of satisfaction and 
security in which all the baby’s depend¬ 
ent needs are being gratified. It is out 
of this most primitive relationship of 
total dependent love that the adult love 
state develops. For the reverse emotion 
we use the terms “anger, rage or hate”, 
to describe a state in which the baby is 
reacting to bodily discomfort, hunger 
and fear and in which his dependent 
needs are not being met. 

The intensity of these two emotions 
arises because, at the most primitive 
level, they relate to the basic instinct 
of self preservation. Whether the young 
one is a kitten, a bird or a human baby, 
it will only live if its parent cares for it 
enough to supply it with food and 
warmth; if the parent rejects it and 
abandons it while it is still helpless and 
dependent, it will die. The kitten mew- 


Toronto, Canada , April , 1957 


27 



ing, the bird squawking and the baby 
bawling for food are motivated by the 
same drive. However, for the human 
baby, the feeding situation is also the 
situation in which he first experiences 
cuddling, caressing and mothering. Very 
quickly the ideas of food and affection 
become linked together; the witholding 
of the one comes to imply the withold¬ 
ing of the other. The baby develops a 
loving attachment to the giver of food 
and affection, the mother; and he turns 
on her the primitive infantile hate and 
rage when she appears to be witholding 
these things. 

The realities of everyday life make 
some periods of frustration and tem¬ 
porary witholding inevitable, so that 
every baby and young child has the 
experiences of both loving and being 
angry with his mother. The quantity 
and quality of these two live experi¬ 
ences as the child continues to develop 
are considered to be important factors 
in the future development of his person¬ 
ality. Guilt enters into the problem of 
dependent love and hate at an early 
stage; this guilt is the anguish and 
self-blame felt by a dependent child 
when he experiences hateful and des¬ 
tructive urges towards the mother 
whom he also loves and needs. It is as 
a result of this conflict that the first 
feelings of depression are experienced. 
When the dependency relationship has 
been only partially satisfactory and 
there has been too much experience of 
hate and frustration and too little of 
love and gratification these feelings with 
guilt may be the core of a state of 
depression, with its mixture of longing, 
loneliness, unsatisfied dependency yearn¬ 
ings and feeling of unworthiness and 
inferiority. 

Therefore, in attempting to reach a 
better understanding of what is going 
on in the minds of our homesick child¬ 


ren, that we may more wisely plan their 
management, we can usefully consider 
the elements that go into the formation 
of infantile depression. 

Classification of Homesickness 

In considering the group of 75 cases, 
we find that they fall roughly into 
three sub-groups, although there is 
naturally some overlapping. 

1 . Homesickness as a natural symptom 
of growing up when the depressive 
feelings arising out of a temporary 
loss of loved ones have not yet been 
accepted but will disappear as soon 
as new substitute loved ones are 
found. 

2. Homesickness due to inadequate 
environmental situations where the 
normal child’s requirements of love 
and dependency are insufficiently 
met and he therefore experiences an 
excess of feelings ranging from un¬ 
familiarity and dissatisfaction to in¬ 
security, destructiveness and hostility. 

3. Homesickness based on faulty parent- 
child relationships , where disturban¬ 
ces are present within the personality 
of the child as a result of existing or 
earlier difficulties in relationship with 
family members. Here love has been 
distorted into anxious dependency; 
and excess hate has been experienced 
and often accompanied by guilt 
feelings. 

(1) The first group in whom home¬ 
sickness occurs as a natural symptom of 
growing up, is probably the most num¬ 
erous. These feelings are inevitably 
experienced by growing children as the 
bond of dependency is loosened and 
they have to separate from their loved 
ones. As a matter of fact, they are 


28 


Canadian Camping 




common feelings to adults also. The 
only difference is that many adults have 
learned to recognize and tolerate them, 
whereas the children are distressed by 
these emotions because they have not 
identified them and do not understand 
what they are really all about. 

Situations do occur which make home 
the important place to be and which 
would make anyone away from home 
wish that they were there. These can 
vary from such normal events as the 
birth of a new baby, to not wanting to 
mirs the visit of some beloved relative 
or not wanting to give up a position on 
the local peewee ball team; or in the 
case of the reluctant adolescent in the 
turmoil of first love, not wanting to take 
the chance of losing out to some rival. 
All of these situations can be very seri¬ 
ous matters and under certain circum¬ 
stances it might be best for the child to 
stay at home or have some special 
arrangement made for at least a visit 
home. More difficult situations crop up 
where one or other parent is seriously 
ill or a divorce is under settlement. 

It is not infrequent to find a situation 
where one child is miserable because he 
knows his parents and his brothers and 
sisters are together having some new 
and different family experience, either 
tripping, travelling or just living in the 
country. 

(2) To turn to the second category, 
environment, which makes the child feel 
less secure than usual, is very familiar 
to us all. The separation by distance 
and difference in routines may cause 
quite a disruption to some children. 
Problems around eating and toileting 
can be very disturbing. The most up¬ 
setting experience to certain children is 
finding themselves among a large, group 
of other children with little or no 
opportunity for privacy. Some children 


seem to be lost with an inability to find 
themselves until they begin to make 
friends and get a sense of belonging. 

(3) In considering the third group, 
children with personality problems and 
disturbed parental relationships, we are 
leading into the more complex cases 
of homesickness. The children being 
referred to now are often basically 
unhappy children, malajusted at home 
and similarly maladjusted away. They 
are dissatisfied with themselves and 
have absorbed the feeling of unworthi¬ 
ness through living with unhappy, un¬ 
satisfied and unsatisfying people. The 
homesickness in these cases does not 
fade with the passage of time. Only 
with an extreme degree of careful un¬ 
derstanding and a great quantity of 
time and effort do some evidences of 
progress appear. 

In exploring the manifestations ol 
homesickness in this group of disturbed 
children, we shall find that we are 
discussing abnormal extremes of the 
same feelings which are to be found in 
all our cases of homesickness. In order 
to understand these more complicated 
problems we shall also find ourselves 
considering the mental mechanisms 
which human beings use to try to pro¬ 
tect themselves from emotional pain 
or discomfort. These are known as 
defense mechanisms”. We all employ 
them to a moderate degree in meeting 
the ups and downs of everyday life. 
They are unhealthy, however, when 
used excessively or inappropriately. 
These defences are often not used 
knowingly by the conscious, thinking 
part of our mind. They operate at the 
level of the unconscious mind, that 
great storehouse of forgotten memories 
and unrecognized drives from which 
many of the motivations for our actions 
spring. 


Toronto , Canada , April , 1957 


29 




The successful accomplishment of 
adjustment requires a satisfactory reso¬ 
lution of the problems of separation 
from home and family. The life exper¬ 
ience of the child up to the time of 
going away may have prepared him 
inadequately for this experience. Into 
this group fall the children who have 
been rendered excessively dependent by 
an overprotective parent, or because of 
their need to hold on to the family 
because of the tenuous ties of excessive 
drive for the child to grow up too fast. 

What . happens inside a child who 
lives in such. ; an atmosphere? In the 
first place, he is made to feel that even 
normal amounts of hostility are very 
wrong feelings for anyone to experience. 
He never learns that one can be angry 
with a loved person without destroying 
the love relationship. He is never al¬ 
lowed to deal with these feelings and 
never has the opportunity to learn to 
tolerate them in himself or others. Yet, 
like all children, he is sometimes going 
to feel hostile* to his parents and since 
many such' children sense the fact that 
they were unwanted, he is especially 
liable to experience such emotions. Be¬ 
cause of the presence of such unper¬ 
mitted feelings, he will begin to regard 
himself as bad and unlovable and will 
become guilty and depressed. In such 
a child, where love has been largely 
replaced by anxious over-dependency, 
memories of fear and hostility out¬ 
balance those of love. When his ex¬ 
cessive dependency is violated by separ¬ 
ation, the feelings of hate and anger 
come flooding into consciousness and 
are extremely difficult to tolerate and 
control. At this point, various defence 
mechanisms may come into play. 

One way in which the child may 
attempt to handle the anger, hate and 
badness which is threatening him from 
within, is by projection. That is to say 


he projects or throws it on to his sur¬ 
roundings. He actually distorts reality 
and sees all those around him as hateful 
and bad people and the surroundings 
as an unpleasant place with inadequate 
facilities. He imagines his home folks 
as benevolent givers and protectors and 
is convinced that they would immedia¬ 
tely come and take him home if they 
only knew how horrible the camp was. 

Other defense mechanisms which may 
be used are repression and denial. Re¬ 
pression is a process by which emotions 
which would result in suffering if cons¬ 
ciously experienced, are censored before 
they even reach the conscious mind. 
They are held down in the unconscious, 
but the effort of holding them down 
absorbs much nervous energy and pro¬ 
duces various undesirable tensions and 
distortions in the emotional life of the 
individual. The allied mechanism of 
denial is one by which a person appears 
to blind himself to what is before his 
eyes and to fail to react appropriately to 
the actual circumstances. 

It is in our youngest children that we 
are more likely to see the use of denial 
and repression. It seems necessary for 
many children of the nursery school 
and kindergarten age to use these de¬ 
fence mechanisms if subjected to separ¬ 
ation from home. For this reason most 
psychiatrists would not support camping 
for this age group unless it was felt 
that the parent-child relationships were 
unsatisfactory and that the camping 
experience would give an opportunity 
to do some reconstructive work with 
the family. In children of this age we 
can sometimes see a “precocious social 
phase” which the untrained eye may 
interpret as a wonderful and succesful 
adjustment to camp. Tim is a form of 
denial and can be a very dangerous 


30 


Canadian Camping 


stage of adjustment in which to remain 
because it acts as a barrier to the form¬ 
ation of any deeper relationships. 

Dr. John Bowlby of the Tavistock 
Clinic in London, sees two ways in 
which repression takes place in the 
preschool age group, when prolonged 
separation occurs. Here the need to be 
mothered or the mental memory or 
image of the mother, or both, can he 
repressed. In the situation of the pre¬ 
cocious social adjustment it is the need 
for mothering that is repressed; often 
the image of mother is also repressed. 
In small children who have taken on a 
very close attachment to a nurse or a 
counsellor as a mother substitute the 
need for a mother is not repressed. 
Sometimes these children make a slip 
of the tongue and call the nurse or 
counsellor “mother” and seem to repress 
the memory of the real mother and 
home. There is a very strange reaction 
to the parent often accompanied by 
confusion or lack of recognition when 
the real mother appears on the scene. 
Talking of home, letters, snap-shots and 
gifts from home and visits from parents 
all help prevent this repression. We all 
recognize, I am sure, the need for 
parental substitutes but we may be less 
aware of the need to help maintain the 
child’s image of his parents. 

Some children are able to express 
some anger but they cannot permit 
themselves to aim it at the real target, 
namely the parents. So they use the 
mechanism of displacement; that is, 
they displace their anger to some less 
vital person or object . 

Other children turn their hostile feel¬ 
ings back to themselves and they may 
be expressed as a sense of unworthiness 
but more frequently they will feel that 
something is wrong with themselves. 
This will often take the form of a physi¬ 
cal complaint. The sleeplessness may 


be a means of preventing horrible night¬ 
mares or bad dreams. 

The child who has experienced too 
much dependency and too little real 
love, requires .excessive material demon¬ 
strations of his worthiness. This is what 
is commonly called greed. He never 
gets satisfied because what he is after 
is love but not knowing what this is, 
he demands its substitutes. These may 
be attention, food or material things. 
The child with a huge truck and sev¬ 
eral bags full of unsuitable things for 
camping may be the tip-off for the 
existence of such a problem.. When he 
gets to camp and finds his supplies of 
“good things” rationed he is in a bad 
way. His old self-protective mechanism 
is threatened so that he will make great 
bids for attention and show everybody 
his fine equipment. If he cannot satisfy 
his greed sufficiently he will become 
overwhelmed with his inner feelings of 
not having “enough good things” within 
himself. He will protect himself as long 
as he can from this intolerable thought 
by building up feelings that everybody 
is after what he has . . . that campers 
and staff are trying to take from him 
all the time . . . that everybody else 
has more privileges than he has. He 
may develop a substitute feeling of envy 
of his fellow campers and will put forth 
every effort possible to be sure to outdo 
them. We may be more familiar with 
this cover-up for not having enough of 
the “good things” in group activities in 
competitive sports, where the team that 
is not quite good enough develops the 
alibi of “that robbing referee”. 

The problems of depression which are 
so common in adolescents can be con¬ 
sidered in the same way, only here they 
are unleashing their former pent-up 
feelings of dependency, hate and anger. 
The more these have been pent up, the

don, England, sums up the feeling of

Sharpe. An English YMCA Secretary 
was showing me around the London

the allocation of space does not permit 
it. It is certain we only go this way 
once. Life moves along at a brisk speed. 
Few of us will ever be in the history 
books. Each person we meet will be 
better or worse from the meeting. Many 
will agree with me that we are better 
for having met C. T. Sharpe. Long may 
we continue to enjoy his friendship.

WILD LIFE CORNER 


By Barry G. Lowes 
Directory Camp New Moon 


Children are alive and inquisitive 
concerning the world about them. Too 
often this natural curiosity is squelched 
at camp. Most camp directors admit 
that they would like to begin a nature 
program, or vitalize a moribund one, 
but plead lack of knowledge. Know¬ 
ledge, while valuable, is not necessary. 
Curiosity is the most important pre¬ 
requisite. With the numerous fine re¬ 
source books available, knowledge can 
be built up. 

This column is designed to offer sug¬ 
gestions that will help to encourage this 
richest area of program. Any sugges¬ 
tions or ideas from readers will be 
gratefully received and acknowledged. 

INSECT TRAP 

Rather than chase all over the coun¬ 
tryside in pursuit of insects, let them 
come to you. The lure is light. 

Simple to set up, an insect trap be¬ 
comes a fascinating doorway into the 
insect world and a favourite night activ¬ 
ity. Any counsellor can do it. Here is 
how. 

Stretch a white sheet between two 
trees, or in a doorway, or hanging from 
a cross-bar, etc. Place a strong source 
of light (e.g.) flashlights, electric bulb, 
a coleman lamp, etc. behind the sheet. 
Wait and watch. 

Soon dozens of different kinds of 
moths and insects attracted by the light 


settle quietly upon the sheet. They are 
easily picked off and placed in a bottle 
that has a small piece of blotting paper 
soaked in carbon tetrachloride at the 
bottom. Kept tightly shut, the fumes 
kill the insects rapidly without injuring 
their wings or colouring. 

STAKING YOUR CLAIM 

This activity teaches observation and 
clearly points up how chock full of life 
the ground really is. 

Each camper stakes his claim to one 
foot of earth. As he digs, he sifts each 
shovel-ful of soil looking for living crea¬ 
tures, grubs, beetles, worms, etc. The 
winner is the one who discovers the 
most in his one-foot claim. This game 
invariably leads to a desire to know 
what has been found; why they are 
underground; their life cycles; what 
they eat, etc.

COUNSELLORS SHOULD SLEEP IN THE SAME ROOM 
WITH THEIR CAMPERS 

The cabin counsellor’s job is the most difficult, demanding and important 
one in camp. It is only natural that at times he should wish to retreat from the 
campers, to be alone, to relax. However, having a room of his own is not the 
answer to the problem. 

How can he relax behind a thin partition with the ominous sounds of cabin 
life impinging upon him? How often must he leave his room to act as mediator? 
Unquestionably, he needs escape. But it must be provided by the camp admini¬ 
stration through days off, evenings off, and as conditions allow, time off during 
the day. 

A counsellor’s room, contiguous with the camper’s is not only an illusory 
escape but it is bought at the expense of camper-counsellor relations. The price 
is too high. 

Program is everything that happens during a camper’s stay at camp. The 
greatest values that any camper derives from camp result from hour-by-hour 
living experiences shared by the whole cabin group. 

that the camper is moulded more by what occurs during these many other hours 

Activity periods are important, no one can deny this, but experience proves 
that the camper is moulded more by what occurs during these many other hours 
of the day. If the guidance of the counsellor is more necessary at one time or 
another, it is during these many “free” hours spent in and around the cabin. To 
divorce the counsellor from this intimate living, sharing contact with the campers, 
is to forfeit all those vital, incomparable opportunities for group living that are 
the major reason for operating our camps. 

Instead of living in constant, friendly, natural contact with his campers, he 
becomes an undeclared “outsider”. The thin partition becomes a wall between 
him and his campers. He must come out of his room in order to be with them. 
Too often his visits are confined to disciplinary sortees. Rather than being an 
integral part of the group, the room widens the gap between them. 

A radio played softly or a small bed lamp for reading are no more disturbing 
at night when the counsellor lives in the same room than if he has his own room. 

Freedom to relax alone, these things he does need, but they can best 
be satisfied by sensibly planned time off. Do not try to purchase this illusory escape 
at the expense of an intimate living relationship. The price that must be paid is 
too high.

COUNSELLORS SLEEP IN THEIR OWN ROOMS 


The counsellor’s principal responsibilities for campers at night center about 
his concern for their safety, his concern for any personal attention they may 
require in case of emergency, and the sense of security a child feels because his 
leader is “close at hand”. 


Counsellors who are required to sleep in the same room as campers, find 
themselves in a situation quite different from that which exists at home. The 
counsellor needs a certain amount of privacy, and his relationship with his campers 
is frequently at a more helpful level if he has “a place to call his own”. In the 
high tempo of camp living, his need also is for a place where he can organize 
his clothing, his books and personal possessions for easy access and quick reference. 


It is assumed that a counsellor will have some free time in the evening. Must 
he then tiptoe in, attempting to ready himself for bed without disturbing his 
campers? If he wishes to write reports or personal letters, must he always go to 
a lounge or writing room where other counsellors write, some read and some just 
cavort around? If he wishes to talk over the day’s activities or problems with 
another counsellor, must he do so in whispers, or in the hearing of his cabin group? 

The counsellor’s room should certainly be in close proximity to the campers’ 
quarters in order to meet the needs indicated in paragraph one. 


The counsellor is not and cannot be “one of the boys”, if he is to perform 
his unique and exacting function. In all fairness to him, let’s give him a room of 
his own. 


Toronto, Canada, April, 1957

REGINA YWCA 

and It’s New Summer Camp 


By Mrs. R. J. Rowe 

Chairman , Regina Y. W. C. A. 

Camh Committee 

For many years, the Regina Y.W.C.A. 
has dreamed of a summer camp to 
meet the needs of girls in the Regina 
Area. Finally, in 1956, this dream was 
realized through co-operation with the 
Regina Kiwanis Club who had oper- 


Director’s cabin. With these facilities, 
the original plan called for three two- 
teen; one for those fourteen and over. 
However, we had very few registrations 
for the seniors, so we decided to aban¬ 
don that camp group and place the few 



ated a camp at Glen Harbour for many 
years, for under-privileged children. 

Since the Kiwanis policy has been to 
build up a project until it is well 
established, and turn it over to some 
other organization to continue its oper¬ 
ation, this site was leased to the 
Y.W.C.A. as a non-sectarian group, to 
organize and operate, the Kiwanis Club 
being responsible for maintenance of 
camp buildings and grounds. 

Fifty-eight miles north of Regina, 
Glen Harbour is situated on beautiful 
Last Mountain Lake, near the town of 
Silton, amid gently rolling prairie hills. 
The cabins on the site provide accom¬ 
modation for a maximum of eighty girls, 
with additional cabins for dining, in¬ 
door activities, sick bay, and Camp 


week periods for girls: one for age ten 
and eleven: one for age twelve and thir- 
older girls who had registered, in the 
intermediate age group. We feel now, 
that in another year, it might be advis¬ 
able to plan two, or even three, camps 
with girls of all ages able to attend each 
camp, since family holidays make it 
difficult for us to accept any certain age 
group for a specific period. 

The fee of twenty-five dollars covered 
the two-week period, and was compared 
with Church and Girl Guide camps 
where all leadership is voluntary. How¬ 
ever, the venture was not too succcsful 
financially, due to the fact that all our 
staff had to be hired. Another year, 
with “Y” staff available, our expenses 
will be cut considerably. Campers reg¬ 
istered from all areas of the city as well 


38 


Canadian Camping 




as from several out-of-town points. 
Among them were thirteen sponsored 
girls so we felt we had a diversity in 
economic and occupational background. 
They all learned to take responsibility 
as members of cabin groups as well as 
in the group as a whole, and every-day 
experiences in daily devotions helped 
them to understand and respect each 
other. 

As to the camp staff: we have a 
Camp Director, Food Services Director, 
Waterfront Counsellor, two Counsellors 
and two Assistant Counsellors. Each 
one had a good camping background, 
and was well able to carry out the 
activities which included swimming and 
water safety instruction, crafts, sports, 
nature lore, cookouts, hikes and stunt 


nights. We also held a special day at 
which Y.W.C.A. World Service was 
interpreted to the girls. Games stem¬ 
ming from various countries were 
played, and quilt blocks were made for 
quilts which were to he sent in parcels 
to World Service Countries. 

For their camping period, campers 
and staff were covered by liability 
insurance. The Camp Director and 
Counsellors held St. John Ambulance 
Certificates, First Aid and Home Nurs¬ 
ing. Two local doctors were on call 
within a short distance of camp in case 
of illness or accident. The camp facili¬ 
ties were approved by the Sanitation 
Inspector, both before and during camp

Tell it To Your 
Campers 

Not only campers but counsellors as 
well, should be keenly alert to the 
dangers an axe of any size or descrip¬ 
tion can present at all times, and should 
be encouraged at every turn to develop 
the utmost respect for this indispensable 
tool. 

Obviously, no canoe trip or cook-out 
hike can be complete without the axe 
to cut firewood, tent poles, saplings for 
shelters or cooking areas, and for many 
other supplies. But however necessary 
it is, strict rules for its use should be 
laid down by the camp director, and by 
the tripping counsellor; it should be 
placed in the hands of experienced 
counsellors only, and of a few senior 
campers who arc thoroughly aware of 
its dangers and potentialities, and who 
can wield it expertly. 

It is Mr. W. J. Stinson of the Ontario 
Department of Lands and Forests who, 
in describing it as the most dangerous 
of cutting tools, suggested ten rules of 
safe use . . . rules which, he said, 

could be followed with advantage 
by cottagers, campers and woodsmen 
everywhere: 

1. Make sure that you are clear of 
others. 

2. Check for obstructions such as 
brush, limbs or lines. 

3. When cutting small brush, hold 
brush firmly with one hand and cut 
away from yourself. 

4. When cutting down a tree, see 
that there are no dead limbs, loose 
objects or leaning trees that may fall 
when the tree is jarred by the axe. 

5. See that everyone, including your¬ 
self. is clear of the tree before it falls. 

6. When limbing a tree, start from 
the butt and, standing on the opposite

WHODUZIT? 


-W. E. (Ted) Yard 

Y.M.C.A. Camp Pinecrest 


How many camp directors have, at 
some time or another, encountered mis¬ 
understanding in staff arrangements 
and responsibilities? Sometimes the mis¬ 
understanding is related to responsibili¬ 
ties . Sometimes it is related to privileges 
and conditions of work . . . sometimes 
even to the amount of remuneration. 

Here is what Hedley S. Dimock calls 
the camp staff: 

— The Spiritual Center of the Camp 
Community. 

— The Value Center of the Camp in 
Operation. 

— The Center for Determining the 
“Educational Destiny” of the Camp. 

— The Chief Center for satisfaction or 
frustration for both campers and 
staff personnel. 


— The Morale Center of the Camp. 

Surely we must have a clear-cut 
agreement with these staff persons who 
are so vital and entirely essential to the 
achievement of our particular object¬ 
ives. 

Many camps use “agreements”, many 
use “contracts”, many use “exchange of 
letters” in confirming staff arrange¬ 
ments. It is not our purpose here to 
hold that any technique is better than 
another, but we present as a basis for 
general consideration, a type of “Staff 
Member’s Agreement” used in one situ¬ 
ation in an effort to establish clear 
understandings at the very beginning of 
important staff relationships. 


NAME OF CAMP 
ADDRESS 

STAFF MEMBER’S AGREEMENT 


Name. Date. 

It is my understanding that I am to serve at Camp. 

for the season beginning.and ending. 

Responsibilities: 

In addition, I will assist in other phases of the camp programme when called 
jpon, according to my ability. 

Remuneration: Board and lodging plus honorarium of.for full

THE GRASS 

GROWS 

GREENER 


By J. B. Liddell 
Camp Mia-Konda 

Lawns are difficult to maintain where 
their use is purely ornamental, but 
where the grass is required for recrea¬ 
tional use or to hold on to banks and 
slopes the problem becomes worse. One 
thing we should be thankful for is that 
our lawn grasses are very tolerant of 
the treatment we give them; give of 
their best under all conditions; and 
thrive in spite of all we do to discourage 
them. 

This brings out one point: if we give 
even token maintenance and care to 
our grass areas they will respond a hun¬ 
dredfold. Fertilizing in spring and fall 
with help and if allowed to go through 
hot, dry spells without cutting they will 
be so much the better. Close cutting is 
one of the main problems grass has to 
contend with. Grass on the average 
lawn should never be cut closer than 
P/ 2 ” allowing it to grow longer in 
shady areas or where heavy traffic will 
cause wear. Remember, too, compac¬ 
tion on heavy soil will cause rapid 
deterioration particularly during periods 
of hot dry weather. 

The establishing and maintenance of 
grass areas is usually a problem of soil 
conditions. Some have sand, others 
gravel or clay. Those with solid rock, of 
course, have no worries. The type of 
soil plus the availability or otherwise of 
a good water supply determine the sort 
of grass we can establish. Cold does 
not enter the picture; luckily all our 
permanent lawn grasses are quite hardy. 
Light soils in the absence of adequate 

Tor onto, Canada, April, 1957 



moisture supplies are the most difficult 
areas in which to establish grass. Light 
gravelly or sandy soils are also usually 
infertile; that is, they lack the normal 
plant foods and are difficult situations 
during periods of drought. Heavy soils, 
on the contrary, tend to hold on to 
moisture, usually have a higher concen¬ 
tration of plant nutrients. They are 
slower to dry out, but will compact 
badly under heavy foot traffic which 
may he a worse condition than drying 
out Both problems can be combatted 
by proper care and maintenance. Re¬ 
member, any crop, grass or otherwise, 
needs feeding for best results, so if your 
grass areas are suffering, perhaps a little 
care may bring them back into shape. 

Good grass areas can be established 
even on difficult soil conditions by sel¬ 
ecting suitable seed mixtures. As I have 
indicated all our permanent lawn grass¬ 
es are hardy, all that is required is a 
variety to suit our particular area. We 
do have a choice. Among the best of 
lawn grasses are Kentucky Blue Grass 
which is best in medium to heavy soils 
where moisture is adequate. Then we 
have the Fescues (Creeping Red Fescue 
and Chewings Fescue) which will with¬ 
stand shade and fairly dry conditions. 
For very dry and gravelly soils Canada 
Bluegrass does well and also thrives on 
clay and very wet soils. With the addi¬ 
tion of a nurse grass (one that germin¬ 
ates quickly but dies out eventually) we 
should be able to make up a mixture 
suitable for all but the most difficult 
areas. 

Cont. next page

in the World!

by

in

HOBBY CRAFT 
2387 Yongc Sf., Toronto - MO. 0967 


The following are suggested basic 
mixtures with rates of sowing from 4 
lbs. to 6 lbs. per 1000 sq. ft. of grass 
area. These mixtures arc not prescribed 
for giving a golf green type of sod. but 
will give a good hard wearing lawn. 

Where water is available:— 

Heavy and Medium Soils: 

60% Kentucky Blue Grass 
20% Creeping Red Fescue 
20% Perennial Rye Grass 
Light Soils: 

50% Kentucky Blue Grass 
30% Creeping Red Fescue 
10% Canada Blue Grass 
10% Red Top 
Where Water is Scarce:— 

Heavy and Medium Soils: 

40% Kentucky Blue Grass 
40% Creeping Red Fescue 
20% Perennial Rye Grass 
Light Soils: 

60% Creeping Red Fescue 
25% Canada Blue 
15% Red Top or Perennial Rye 
Good preparation of the site is most 
important, giving the grass a good start. 
Adequate moisture during the germina¬ 
tion period is a must if a good catch is 
to be expected. In every instance a low 
nitrogen fertilizer such as 2-12-10 or 
20% Superphosphates should be worked 
into the top inch or two of the soil 
before sowing. Rates of between 20 
lbs. and 30 lbs. per 1000 sq. ft. of 
grass area should be adequate. 

Fall sowing in Eastern Canada and 
British Columbia is usually best, but 
experience has shown that the best 
time for sowing in the Prairie Provinces 
is in the spring. This note is only a 
guide to the general principles of grass 
growing. There is a great deal more to 
it than this. Where large areas are in¬ 
volved it is wise to submit soil samples 
to the Department of Soils at your local 
Agricultural College with a full state¬ 
ment of conditions pertaining to your 
area. They will be happy to give you 
advice and recommend suitable seed 
mixtures and fertilizers.

Canoeing, 




cA Canadian J4e%itag.e 

By Mary Porter 



PART II —ITS HISTORY AND DEVELOPMENT 


The history of exploration in Canada, 
is intimately linked with the canoe. 
Champlain explored the Ottawa, Nip- 
issing and French Rivers as well as 
Georgian Bay, the Huron country and 
Lake Ontario, all by canoe. The Algon¬ 
quin Story contains an exciting descrip¬ 
tion of his travels. He frankly admitted 
that the canoe was better suited to 
Canadian travel than the long-boat and 
skiff in which he had made a trip to 
Lachine Rapids. 

The two major tasks in the explora¬ 
tions of the seventeenth century were to 
discover the water route between the 
Saint Lawrence River and Hudson Bay 


and the water route west from Lake 
Superior to the western Great Lakes. 
Simon and dTberville reached James 
Bay by canoe and claimed Hudson Bay 
for France. The latter task was com¬ 
pleted bv Verendrye, a fur trader, 
around 1731. Thus, exploration, canoe¬ 
ing, and development of the fur trade 
seem to go hand in hand. 

Competition for furs between the 
Hudson’s Bay Company and the North 
West Company was keen. The large 
“voyageur” canoes were penetrating 
deeper into the interior of the country, 
carrying heavy supplies west, and car¬ 
goes of furs east. The Nor’ Wester 


Toronto, Canada, April, 1957

WINDSOR MATTRESS

673 CARON AVENUE 

WINDSOR, ONTARIO 


route was by way of the Ottawa River, 
Lake Nipissing and French River to 
Georgian Bay, along the north shores 
of lakes Huron and Superior to the 
Kamimistiquia River. The fort there 
was the noted meeting place of the fur 
trade, and the gateway to the western 
lakes and rivers of the Indian territories. 
The explorations of Alexander Mac¬ 
kenzie, the greatest Nor’ Wester, to the 
Arctic and Pacific stand out amongst 
the most remarkable achievements of 
Canadians. He was the first white man 
to reach the Pacific Ocean by the over¬ 
land route. 

Canoes made it possible for the early 
French invaders to settle along the 
shores of the St. Lawrence, and for the 
missionaries to carry their gospel to the 
so-called savages of the interior. The 
Jesuit, Brebeuf, travelled the Ottawa- 
Nipissing route into the Huron country. 
Many missionaries travelled with the 
explorers as Father Galinee did with 
La Salle in 1669. Another Jesuit, Father 
Marquette accompanied Louis Joliet in 
his explorations and discovered the con¬ 
nection between the St. Lawrence and 
Mississippi Rivers. 

Several explorers described a strange 
type of skin canoe which they saw on 
their northern trips. This was probably 
the “kayak” or “oomiak” of the Arctic 
Eskimo; the fourth type of canoe native 
to Canada. It consisted of sealskin 
stretched over a framework of wood or 
whalebone. The covered deck protected 
the traveler against the cold Arctic 
winds. The modern kayak, with both 
single and double cockpits is used in 
many Olympic Games’ events. It is 
more sharply pointed than the Cana¬ 
dian type and resembles a racing shell 
in shape. The paddler sits low in the 
craft and uses a double paddle. It has 
a covered deck and a small cockpit. 

By the beginning of the nineteenth 
century the canoe was meeting compe- 



48 


Canadian Camping 




tition in the East from the flat-bottomed 
batteau, which was used particularly by 
the incoming United Empire Loyalists. 
The North West Company adopted the 
batteau because it carried more freight 
than the canoe. In 1821 The North 
West Company was absorbed by the 
Hudson’s Bay Company and George 
Simpson replaced the canoe with the 
“York Boat”, a Norwegian type vessel. 
It became the freight-carrying vessel 
west of Lake Superior. Further com¬ 
petition for the canoe was the “Durham 
Boat”, introduced on the St. Lawrence 
by the Americans. This flat-bottomed 
barge was eighty feet long, had a ten 
foot beam and was propelled by sails. 

The Loyalists and later travelers also 
used the “Schenectady Boat”, a varia¬ 
tion of the batteau. These small flat- 
bottomed boats were used in the early 
mail service between Kingston, York 
and Niagara. However, even the bat- 
teaux were eventually replaced by the 
large paddle-wheeled steamships. The 
light canoe was retained for pageantry 
and swift passenger travel. One such 
pageant of voyageurs in their canoes 
was staged by Sir George Simpson for 
the Prince of Wales when he visited 
Canada in 1860. This was said to have 
influenced his decision to become Com¬ 
modore of the Royal Canoe Club, the 
progenitor of the British Canoe Associa¬ 
tion. 

Many changing conditions affected 
canoe travel in Canada. Woods were 
cleared for settlement, thus driving the 
fur-bearing animals further into the 
interior. The fur-trade was less profit¬ 
able since silk was displacing beaver as 


the vogue in Europe. The building of 
roads and the Canadian Pacific Rail¬ 
way sped up overland travel, while the 
opening of canals facilitated the steam¬ 
ship routes on the Great Lakes. Even 
the Indians, formerly a migratory 
people, were now confined to reserves 
without excuse for travel. The birch- 
bark canoe was replaced by the stronger 
cedar strip craft in Ontario and the 
chestnut canoe in the Maritimes. In 
the far north the canvas canoe became 
popular because it is easily repaired. 
Peterborough, Ontario and Fredericton, 
New Brunswick became the new canoe- 
building centres of Canada. 



These adverse conditions did not 
eliminate the canoe from our country 
but merely changed the nature of its 
course. The canoe still remains in the 
hearts and lives of vacationer, woods¬ 
man and camper as the safest and most 
enjoyable small craft in existence. 

(To be concluded in the June issue)

Camping Association Office.

1957 CAMP REFERENCE 
AND BUYING GUIDE 

Compiled by the Editors of Camping 
Magazine. 

Almost anyone who expects to have 
anything to do with operating or work¬ 
ing in a camp will find value in this 
10th anniversary edition of the Camp 
Reference and Buying Guide. The 
book’s more than 150 pages are 
crammed with a wide variety of factual 
answers to questions likely to come up 
in the course of a camping season. 

The book is divided into sections on 
Business Management, Food and Food 
Service, Health and Safety, Mainten¬ 
ance and Development, and Program. 
Each section is further subdivided to 
cover a wide range of activities. 

For example, the Program section 
contains information on more than 200 
different craft projects, graded by age 
of camper and with list of materials 
required. Also covered under Program 
are photography, boat mooring meth¬ 
ods, equipment for camp waterfronts, 
dock layouts, pool maintenance meth¬ 
ods, dimensions and diagrams of fields 
and courts for most popular camp 
sports, check-list of sports supplies, 


riflery pointers, graded tests of camping 
skills, equipment for out-of-camp trips, 
camp movies, etc. Other sections are 
similarly comprehensively covered. 

Included also are a bibliography of 
over 300 books in the field of camping; 
a section on the American Camping 
Association, of which the Camp Refer¬ 
ence and Buying Guide is an official 
publication; and the Buying Guide 
which lists hundreds of sources from 
which can be obtained nearly every 
product needed in the operation of a 
camp. Galloway Publishing Co., 120 
West 7th Street, Plainfield, N.J. $2 


STORY TALKS FROM 
ANIMAL LIFE 

Jacob J. Sessler 

Do you know that a butterfly drinks 
through its tongue (as we use a straw), 
and why? Or that the worms on a farm 
weigh more than all the other animals 
—cows, horses, pigs, sheep, chickens— 
put together? Mr. Sessler tells us there 
are 1 to 2 million in an acre of farm¬ 
land, an astounding thought indeed! 
Children will be intrigued with his ac¬ 
count of the kangaroo which is barely 
one inch long at birth, the giraffe which 


50 


Canadian Camping 


is born 5 feet tall, can walk on his first 
day, and can outdistance a lion when 
only a few days old. Here is a collection 
of 35 short stories for children about 
animal life, by a man who believes that 
children can be instructed in the great 
truths by the use of nature’s symbols 
and illustrations, thus bringing universal 
themes into the framework of the 
child’s interest and comprehension. He 
shows us the lion cubs with their 
mother and then points out how we too 
can learn from those older and wiser 
than ourselves; he tells us that the 
bumblebee is the only creature who can 
reach the nectar of the red clover, thus 
helping to propogate what is the essen¬ 
tial food for cows, clover hay, which 
demonstrates that while a job may seem 
small it is important and should be 
done well. 

Each chapter is a complete story in 
itself, taking about 5 minutes to read 
aloud. A leader might like to edit the 
material or apply it in his own way. 
For instance, I personally would find it 
a little out of character for me to say, 
“God made the lion in order that there 
would not he too many zebras”, or 
“When God saw how short the zebra’s 
neck was, he decided to give him a long 
head so he could reach down to eat 
grass”. When he says, “While we may 
not know why God made the mosqui¬ 
toes, at least in the mosquito He has 
shown us what wonderful things He 
can do”, every camper will nod with 
understanding! G. R. Welch Co. Ltd., 
Toronto. $2

BE PREPARED! (The Life and 
Illusions of a Scoutmaster) 

Rice E. Cochran 

Not to be confused with the official 
handbook on scouting, of similar title, 
that addition of an exclamation mark 
prepares us for a glimpse of what is 
going on under the scoutmaster’s hat 
—and perhaps more especially behind 
his back. Illustrated by amusing line 
drawings by Robert Osborn, Scoutmas¬ 
ter Cochran’s twenty years experience 
is his background for yarning in a 
thoroughly entertaining and often very 
helpful vein about everything from 
“How to toughen Tenderfeet”, the 
handy guide he’d like to offer parents, 
that maddening staff, at the National 
office, to jamborees and so forth. 

There is nothing like a refreshing 
draught of humour to relax and reas¬ 
sure those who face problems and frus¬ 
tration in their efforts to do a good job. 
By sharing with us his anecdotes of 
almost every kind of triumph and trag¬ 
edy that can assail a Scoutmaster and 
his troup, he helps bring a new per¬ 
spective, too, on the very real satisfac¬ 
tions that can be found in working with 
that infuriating and fascinating aggre¬ 
gation of humanity — the boy scout 
troop, or for that matter any group of 
boys. G. J. McLeod, Toronto. $4
