Toronto, Canada, April, 1957 


53 




continued from page 21 


D. You will be expected to maintain 
Discipline. Keep him busy—“Satan 
finds things for idle hands to do”. 
Perhaps he does need to sit on a rock 
and just think. But try to give him 
something worthwhile to think about, 
while he’s sitting on that rock. 

E. You will be expected to be dis¬ 
criminating in what you teach the 
camper. 

Children are learning all the time 
—observation and imitation. Conse¬ 
quently when you are with them you 
are teaching them. The way you 
look; the way you act; the way you 
talk and the things you say. You 
cannot say “Now, I’m teaching — 
now I’m jio.t”. 

This “monkey see, monkey do” 
side of children’s nature is something 
parents learn about quickly — some¬ 
times it is difficult for counsellors. 

And so, you are teaching aesthetic 
appreciation; attitudes towards 
people and life. You are teaching 
posture and speech. You are teaching 
ethics and the principles of demo¬ 
cracy. A word you speak may linger 
forever in the minds of these child¬ 
ren. Teachers are always being re¬ 
minded of this. 

Counsellors must weigh and mea¬ 
sure, and decide what are the good 
things, and what are the worthwhile 
things which are going to make this 
child’s life richer. Help the camper 
learn to love the outdoors—to appre¬ 
ciate it, to live in it. 

But keep it simple. Give it to him 
in his own terms. If it was his turn 
to empty the waste basket don’t 


launch into a theoretical harangue 
on democracy. Teach him what he 
is ready to learn — you wouldn’t 
teach a non-swimmer to do a swan 
dive. 

A ten year old doesn’t comprehend 
your personal problems. Unless they 
are within his powers to understand, 
they only be-fuddle the clean simple 
line of communication between you 
and him. 

This goes for your philosophy of 
life too. Late adolescence and young 
adulthood is a time of questioning, 
and searching for knowledge, for 
tearing down all the existing struc¬ 
tures of society and trying to find a 
way of building them up again. This 
is normal for you. You’d be stupid 
and unthinking if you didn’t do this. 
But children are not yet ready for 
this. Don’t force young, unprepared 
minds to cope with something they 
have no techniques to deal with. 
Aborigines can’t learn how to behave 
in a ball room in one easy lesson. A 
horrified parent says “My Johnny 
says his counsellor doesn’t believe in 
God”. (A child will not he ready for 
a discussion of this kind until he’s 
older). 


F. You will be expected to MAKE IT 
FUN. 

Please remember: you are working 
with human material. The most prec¬ 
ious segment of it . . . the nation’s 
children . . . the hopes of the future. 

Yours is a twenty-four-hour-a-day 
job. What will you get out of it? The 
more you give, the more you get!

Some of Miss Mary Edgar’s most enchanting poems were written especially for the early 
issues of Canadian Camping. Touched with whimsy and generously brushed with humour, 
they have an appeal to both camper and counsellor. Rare gems, these, since they are not 
available in book form; so we offer them here as an addition to your collection of Woodfire 
and Candle-light readings. 


THE CAMPER AND THE 
BIRTHDAY SUIT 

Once there was a camper 
Whose first letter to her home 
Amazed her doting parents 
And inspired this little “pome”. 

(She wrote) : 

Dear Mum and Dad: Got here O.K., 
Please send a box of food. 

My cabin mates inform me 
There is swimming “a la nude”. 

They say my bathing suit won’t do, 

It’s not the kind they wear; 

Please buy for me a Birthday Suit, 

And rush it here by air. 


LIFESAVING 

Once there was a camper 
And it was her boastful aim, 

All life-saving tests to pass, 

And thus achieve much fame. 

Her “Buddy” practised with her 
And clutched her with such vim, 

She shrieked: “I much prefer to drown 
Than be saved by means so grim”. 


THE CAMPER AND THE 
SOAP FLAKES 

Once there was a camper 
Not too bright, alas, alack! 

She stuffed her bag with laundry 
And heaved it on her back. 

She called to all her cabin mates 
“I’m off to wash my clothes , 
Shirts and shorts and hankies, 
Underthings and hose.” 

Down to the shore she gaily tripped, 
But this was her mistake: 

Her box of powdered soap-flakes 
She sprinkled in the lake! 


TABLE TALK 

Once there was a camper 
And her counsellor heard her say 
To the campers at her table 
In the dining room one day: 
“The meals we get are very good, 
I’m really quite surprised ; 

It’s such a great relief to know 
The milk is paralyzed ” 


Toronto, Canada, April, 1957

ON SELECTING STAFF 
FOR 

JUNIOR CAMP 

By E. Flynn 


Gomes this time of year and camp 
directors are in the throes of staff se¬ 
lection. The search for senior members 
is exacting enough, but when it comes 
to staffing a, camp for the youngest of 
campers ... the five-to-eight-year-olds 
. . . it’s like looking for angels on a 
nearby cloud. 

Counsellors for Junior Camp are a 
breed unto themselves. Their chrono¬ 
logical age doesn’t seem to enter the 
picture at all. A young person of eigh¬ 
teen or so may or may not be the 
kind of person who is aware of the 
constant needs of these tiny children; 
he may not think at the campers’ level; 
he may expect too much of the campers, 
both .physically and emotionally. A per¬ 
son who is past fifty may still be far 
from that state of maturity which places 
the needs of others ahead of his own. 
Anyone, of any age, may be the in¬ 
spired, and inspiring, leader for older 
campers, yet possess not a whit of talent 
for handling small ones. On the other 
hand, we have all known people . . . 
they may be eighteen, thirty-five-ish or 
sixty . . . who are blessed with that 
precious sixth sense which can cope 
with tiny tots just like that. These 
people, ever on the alert, have what it 
takes to give small campers a summer 
of fun and new learning, and good 


health; all this, and an intangible some¬ 
thing else, too. 

What should a director look for when 
he selects his Junior Camp counsellors? 

Before a reliable staff can be assem¬ 
bled, a definite conception of what he 
wants his counsellors to he must exist 
in the director’s mind. Surely the first 
requisite is a capacity to create a happy, 
relaxed atmosphere in the whole section. 
Counsellors should, of course be in good 
health, and possess the kind of strong 
constitution that takes what comes as 
a matter of course, one that quickly 
adjusts to any contingency. The direc¬ 
tor will expect his counsellors to run 
the section efficiently and effectively; 
he will hope that his staff will be loyal 
to his philosophy of camping, to his 
concept of the results a programme 
should bring, to his theory that “camp 
is for the campers”. He will certainly 
hope that his campers, through the 
enjoyment th£ counsellors have created, 
will go home with a love of their camp- 
mates, a respect for the Wide Open 
Spaces, and a keen ctesire for summer 
after summer of camp life. 

This is only the beginning. Over and 
above all other qualities, skills and vir-

tues, those in charge of this section must 
possess a genuine love for small child¬ 
ren. This is not a worthless, sentimental 
kind of attachment. Rather is it the 
kind of relationship which calls for an 
understanding of their needs, then am¬ 
bitions, their frustrations. It is the kind 
of affection which survives the camping 
period through thick and thin, over¬ 
looks faults or slights, endures through 
the child’s trials and tribulations, and 
rejoices with his triumphs. 

If an interview reveals that a staff 
member does not like camp living in 
all winds and weather, if he prefers 
the conveniences of city accommodation 
to a cabin or tent in the woods where 
the only running water is the lake, if 
he is not willing to attend to his charges 
at ANY hour of the day or night, then 
his place is not at camp, least of all in 
Junior section. Bear in mind that this 
person must himself feel at home in the 
woods if his campers are to absorb an 
enthusiasm he should possess, 

A sense of humour is the velvet glove 
one needs always to temper the inevi¬ 
table ups and downs of camp life. With¬ 
out it, many a good jest is lost; with it, 
no enthusiasm can be dampened, no 
task is too discouraging. A true sense 
of humour, completely devoid of sar¬ 
casm, teaches children to laugh at them¬ 
selves, and counsellors to view them¬ 
selves less seriously. 

Then there is patience. Who can 
survive a summer ... or an activity 
. . . without it? In this age group, 
patience means, again, comprehension 
. . . that these small campers are not 
far beyond the primary stage of mus¬ 
cular development; that they cannot 
take long periods of activity; that they 
cannot sit still for as long as five min¬ 
utes sometimes; that they cannot attain 
the degree of perfection older children 
reach with ease. The prospective coun¬ 
sellor should be well endowed with this 
virtue. 

Cont. next page 
Canadian Camping 




Through questioning the applicant, 
the director can try to determine 
whether or not there is present in that 
person’s make-up a sense of awareness 
that appreciates: 

The childrens* capacity for excite¬ 
ment. 

Their need for rest. 

The point at which they are too cold 
to stay in the water. 

Their need for certain foods. 

Their need for extra bedding at night. 

Their need for certain cabin mates 
and not others. 

Their need for the attention of doctor 
or nurse. 

Their need for recognition, for praise, 
for encouragement. 

Does this presuppose that all Junior 
Camp counsellors must have special 
training or hold University Degrees, or 
certificates from this or that course? 

As it is in anv other business or pro¬ 
fession, so it is in camp counselling. 
University training does provide stu¬ 
dents with an opportunity to think, 
observe, study and discuss. A course in 
Childhood Management teaches tech¬ 
niques for handling children and pro¬ 
motes extensive study in child psychol¬ 
ogy. But these are not the only criteria. 
The right kind of experience gained 
through actual work with small child¬ 
ren can, in many cases, supersede book¬ 
training without experience. There are 
countless directors who choose from 
among their applicants those fine people 
who have been actively engaged in 
nursery school or creche work, those 
who have had extensive Sunday School 
training, or who are elder sisters or 
brothers in large families where respon¬ 
sibility for the younger members has 
been on their shoulders. Yet none of 
these may ever have been inside a 
University. They are, of course, well- 
read, intelligent people who possess 
most of the qualities outlined herein.

continued from page 59 

The ideal counsellor, perhaps, is a 
mature type of person of even tempera¬ 
ment and quiet manner, who is experi¬ 
enced in the field of children’s work, 
preferably one who holds a University 
degree in Physical Education, Physical 
or Occupational Therapy, Nursing, So¬ 
cial Work, Child Psychology, Music or 
Arts and Crafts. The person who heads 
up a section or an activity is usually 
found to hold a standing comparable 
to this. 

Some counsellors, and very efficient 
ones, are married women . . . some¬ 
times a married couple . . . who 

have, or who are at present, bringing 
up a family. It is imperative however, 
that as a staff member, this person can 
be entirely objective about her own 
children. She will, too, be able to give 
a much richer experience to her camp¬ 
ers, and she will be more relaxed if 
her own children are old enough to 
live with an age group other than 
Juniors. 

Need we mention that the prospec¬ 
tive counsellor should be fastidious, 
prompt, careful of his manner of speak¬ 
ing as well as in what he says? Need 
we say that he should possess good 
judgement, be fair in his dealings, and 
poised enough to take teasing from his 
campers, play in their games with them, 
have fun with them, yet know how to 
stop at that Right Moment before the 
group gets out of hand? 

A camping experience is every child’s 
birthright. Counsellors can make or 
mar a whole summer, a whole life, an 
entire outlook. A few facts faced dur¬ 
ing the interview, a little time devoted 
to thought before reaching a decision 
to employ an applicant, may provide all 
the good things campers should have 
. . . especially when they are Juniors. 

— • 


Medical Forms 

It is only recently that great strides 
have been made in the medical world 
with the introduction of the Salk Polio 
Vaccine, to the extent that a great 
many campers may have received their 
required shots during the school year. 

Since directors are constantly con¬ 
cerned with the threat of Polio, it 
would make things easier for them and 
for the medical staff if parents could 
make this information available. Why 
not include the question on your Medi¬ 
cal Form this year: “Has your child 
received Polio Vaccine? If so, how 
many shots?” 

Another question which would assist 
the camp doctor is this: “Is your child 
allergic to certain antibiotics, such as, 
Penicillin, Sulpha, Tetanus Anti-toxin?” 

If you have already printed your 
Medical Forms for this year, it might 
be worthwhile to attach a mimeo¬ 
graphed memo, asking these two ques¬ 
tions.

C. Be prompt in attendance at camp activities. 

1. On time for meals. 

2. On time at scheduled meetings. 

D. Abide by necessary regulations. 

1. No swimming without a lifeguard supervising; no swimming after dark. 

2. Staff members are expected to remain on camp property unless on day 
off, or having made specific clearance with section head. 

3. Any person wilfully damaging, mutilating, or abusing camp or personal 
property is responsible for restoring such property. 

4. Staff members who smoke are asked to refrain from doing so in the 
presence of campers. 

5. Private cars are not brought to camp except by written permission of 
Camp Committee. 

E. Be careful and prompt in completion of required records. 

1. Complete and turn in on time all records relating to the campers under 
your supervision. 

2. Keep accurate account of money, supplies and equipment placed in your 

care. —#

NOTES ON INSURANCE 
E. C. Labbett 

It is a known fact that millions of 
dollars are fleeced from unsuspecting 
employers each year in every type of 
business by so-called “honest” employees. 
You, as a camp director or owner, 
would not hire a person for any trusted 
position unless you could trust him. 
The above employers trusted their staff 
members until they found out, to their 
utter dismay, that the books had been 
“fixed” or the cash box was short 
. . . when it was too late to do any¬ 
thing about the situation. A Fidelity 
Bond is the answer . . . the premium 
is low, and any amount of protection 
may be procured. This policy protects 
you against possible dishonest acts of 
employees, should they illegally take 
money, securities or merchandise. It 
also gives you an added check on your 
employee, since the Bonding Company 
will not issue a bond on an individual 
until they have investigated that per¬ 
son and found him to be reliable. 

A note re Building Alterations — 

Your attention is drawn to Clause 5 
(a) of the Statutory Conditions of 
every Fire Insurance Policy. It reads 
as follows—“Unless permission is given 
by the policy or endorsed thereon, the 
insurer shall not be liable for loss or 
damage occurring: (a) to buildings or 
their contents during alteration or re¬ 
pair of the buildings and in conse¬ 
quence thereof; fifteen days being al¬ 
lowed in each year for incidental 
alterations or repairs without such per¬ 
mission.” Look to the wording on the 
face of your policies to see if this 
standard clause is altered in any way. 
Always Remember — 

Your insurance agent represents 
you, not the company. He receives his 
compensation in the form of commis¬ 
sion from the premium you pay to the 
company. If you have any questions 
about insurance, contact your agent; if 
he does not know the answer, he knows 
where to find it. He will be happy to 
be of service. Call upon him as you 
would your family doctor.

continued from page 40 

side to that which you are limbing, with 
your back to the top of the tree. 

7. Cut the limbs close to the trunk 
and from the butt side of the tree. 

8. If the tree is up ofT the ground, 
make sure your toes are not protruding 
under and in the path of the axe. 

9. When cutting dead wood, be care¬ 
ful of hollow or rotted sections that will 
allow the axe to pass through freely 
with great force. 

10. A moment’s thought may be a 
great contribution towards the preven¬ 
tion of “Ax-i-dents”. 

As a guide when instructing the inex¬ 
perienced, Mr. Stinson suggested: 

1. When choosing a pole or single- 
bitted axe, choose a good axe head— 
one balanced slightly heavier on the bit 
side of the eye. 

2. Check the pole or back for splin¬ 
ters or mushroom cfTect. 

3. Check the bit for nicks and make 
sure it is ground with a good taper and 
that the bit has no shoulders. 

4. Choose a straight, sound hard¬ 
wood handle without cracks or splinters. 

5. Make sure the head is proper¬ 
ly hung on the handle and securely 
wedged. 

6. Keep head end of handle oiled; 
this serves to keep the head tight on the 
handle by swelling the wood. 

7. Keep the head free from rust and 
the handle free from gum or grease. 

8. Keep the axe away from young 
children. 

9. Never lay the axe where anyone 
may step on it. 

10. Keep a protective guard on the 
bit of the axe when not in use.

BIRD CHARTS 

Two certain ways to increase interest 
in bird identification are: 


1. Give each camper a bird check list, 
secured for 2$ each from the Royal 
Ontario Museum. There is real 
satisfaction in being able to check a 
new bird that is a “first” on a 
camper’s list. 

2. Make a large bird chart that can be 
posted on the nature bulletin board.

many different birds will be recorded 


during any season. (75 to 100 is com¬ 
mon)

let us hear about them so that they may 
be shared with others.

his own instruments such as scalpel, 
special forceps, scissors, suturing need¬ 
les, ear curettes, special syringes, rubber 
gloves, tourniquet, oral thermometer 
and such special materials as adrenahn, 


local anaesthetic, narcotic drugs, peni¬ 
cillin for injection, etc. He would pro¬ 
bably also provide anaesthetic material^ 
ampules of saline or glucose solution, 
and would order intravenous sets if 
indicated. Elastic Adhesive Bandages 
and Plaster Bandages would also be 
best provided by the physician in 
attendance.
